Cross-fitted partially linear regression (double machine learning)

Source: R/pollution.R
plrcf.Rd

Estimates the effect of a continuous exposure (or treatment) on an outcome after adjusting for confounders, by the double machine learning recipe: the part of the outcome and of the exposure that the confounders predict is removed with models fitted on other folds of the data, and the effect is the slope of what is left. It answers questions such as “how much does asthma incidence rise per microgram of NO2, holding income and age structure fixed?”.

Usage

plrcf(data, y, trt, covs, kfol = 5L, seed = 1L)

Arguments

data

A data frame with one row per unit.

y, trt

Column names (single strings) of the outcome and of the continuous treatment or exposure; both numeric.

covs

Column names of the confounders (one or more strings), numeric. Code a categorical confounder as indicator columns first.

kfol

Number of cross-fitting folds, a whole number of at least 2 (default 5).

seed

Seed of the fold assignment (default 1), so the estimate is reproducible.

Value

A list with ate (the estimate of \(\theta\): the change in the outcome per unit of the treatment), se (its sandwich standard error), n (complete rows used), kfol and method (a string naming the estimator).

Details

The partially linear model \(Y = \theta D + g(X) + U\), \(D = m(X) + V\) of Chernozhukov et al. (2018, section 4.2), estimated by the DML2 cross-fitting recipe: the sample is split into kfol folds; for each fold the nuisances \(m\) and \(g\) are fitted on the other folds and predicted on it; \(\hat\theta\) is the slope of the out-of-fold outcome residuals on the out-of-fold treatment residuals, $$\hat\theta = \sum_i \hat V_i \hat U_i / \sum_i \hat V_i^2,$$ with the sandwich standard error \(\sqrt{\sum_i \hat V_i^2 (\hat U_i - \hat\theta \hat V_i)^2} / \sum_i \hat V_i^2\). The nuisances here are ordinary least squares on the covariates, which is the right learner when the confounding is approximately linear and keeps the estimator fully deterministic given seed; rmorie's morie_estimate_double_ml() offers richer learners and can be passed to exprspplr through estimator.

Each fold's two least-squares fits are computed from the normal equations of the covariates centred and scaled by their full-sample moments (the same column space, so the same fitted values as lm.fit), solved by Cholesky; a fold whose cross-product is poorly conditioned (reciprocal condition number below 1e-5: collinear covariates or a constant column) uses lm.fit instead, whose pivoting drops the redundant columns (their coefficients count as 0). An n = 20000 fit takes a few milliseconds. A bar on stderr shows the folds when the work is slow enough to need one (see blprog).

Rows with a missing value in any of the named columns are dropped first (n reports the rows used). The folds are a random permutation of rep_len(1:kfol, n) drawn with seed; R's own random stream is restored afterwards. Refusals: a column name that is not a single string (several for covs) or is not in data; a non-numeric column (a factor is not a code); kfol that is not a whole number of at least 2; fewer than 2 * kfol complete rows; and a treatment with no variation left after the covariates are partialled out.

References

Chernozhukov, V., Chetverikov, D., Demirer, M., Duflo, E., Hansen, C., Newey, W. and Robins, J. (2018). Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters. The Econometrics Journal 21(1), C1-C68.

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(200), x2 = rnorm(200))
d$exposure <- 20 + 2 * d$x1 + rnorm(200)
d$asthma <- 5 + 0.3 * d$exposure + d$x2 + rnorm(200)
fit <- plrcf(d, "asthma", "exposure", c("x1", "x2"))
fit$ate
#> [1] 0.2536464

# A 95 percent normal confidence interval from the standard error.
fit$ate + c(-1.96, 1.96) * fit$se
#> [1] 0.1156209 0.3916718

# The fold split changes the estimate a little; ten folds instead of five.
plrcf(d, "asthma", "exposure", c("x1", "x2"), kfol = 10, seed = 2)$ate
#> [1] 0.2676102

# A text column is refused rather than read as codes.
d$region <- sample(c("north", "south"), 200, replace = TRUE)
try(plrcf(d, "asthma", "exposure", c("x1", "region")))
#> Error : column `region` must be numeric (a factor or character column is not a code)
